segments.text: Here is a puzzle that has ended campaigns.
A truck is sent to carry fuel to an army 500 commoners away.
To get there, the truck has to burn some of the fuel it carries.
So a second truck is sent to carry fuel for the first one, and that truck burns fuel
too.
Keep going, and a strange thing happens.
The farther the army is from home, the more of every load is simply the cost of carrying
the load, and the less is left for anyone to fight with.
That small trap is the whole subject of this video.
The question is how an army that has hundreds or thousands of comolitors from its factories
keeps getting what it needs, which is fuel, ammunition, food, water, and spare parts, in
the right place on the right day.
We will follow one load from the factory to the front and look at each stage in turn.
Every stage exists because the one before it could not finish the job, and each one hands
the army a new problem.
Start where the load is largest and the distance is longest.
Armies move almost everything that matters by sea and by rail first.
One cargo ship carries what thousands of trucks could not, burns far less fuel for each ton,
and needs a few dozen sailors instead of thousands of drivers.
A train does the same on land.
This is the cheapest way there is to move weight over distance, and that is why every army begins
here.
Its flaw is just as plain.
Ships need ports, and trains need track.
So both can only go where the infrastructure already exists, and both end at a fixed point
on a map, which is exactly where the enemy will look.
In June 1944, the Allies landed in Normandy with a plan that leaned on a big port.
The nearest one, Cherbourg, fell late in the month, and the Germans had wrecked it so thoroughly
that it took weeks to bring back.
So the Allies towed in prefabricated concrete harbors, the Mulberries, and for a while landed
supplies over open beaches.
A harbor delivered on a tow line is the most expensive answer to a missing port, and the
best proof of how far an army will go to avoid being without one.
The port or the railhead is only where the load stops being cheap.
From there it has to cross land that has no ships or rails, and the only thing that does
that at scale is the truck.
Trucks are slow and thirsty compared with a ship, but they go anywhere with a road, and
they can be added by the hundred.
In late summer of 1944, the American army racing across France faster than its planners had
expected, built a truck route called the Red Ball Express.
At its peak, it ran several thousand trucks around the clock, on one-way roads reserved
for it, and delivered thousands of tons a day.
It also showed the trap from the start of this video.
As the front moved away from Normandy, the round trip got longer, and by some accounts
a growing share of the fuel on those trucks was burned just to deliver the rest.
The route was never meant to last.
It was a bridge across a gap, and it worked mainly because the gap was short enough, and
the war was close to its end in France.
There is one more way to move a load, and it is the one nobody can afford for long.
An aircraft needs no road, no port, and no railway, which is why the Berlin Airlift of 1948
and 1949 could keep a blockaded city alive.
But a cargo aircraft carries a small fraction of what a train carries, and burns more fuel doing
it. Air is how an army moves the things it cannot wait for.
It is not how an army feeds itself.
That is the arithmetic every logistician fears.
Each extra kilometer between the supply point and the fighting does not add a little to
the cost.
It adds to the number of trucks, which adds to the fuel they burn, the drivers they need,
the spare parts they use up, and the road they wear out.
You cannot fix it by buying more trucks, because more trucks make the sum worse.
So the fix is almost always to shorten the distance instead.
Repair the railway and push the railhead forward.
Lay a pipeline, as the Allies did in 1944, even running one under the English Channel, because
a pipe has no drivers and burns nothing to push fuel along.
Move the depot forward as the front moves, then move it again, and keep the trucks doing
short and frequent hops.
Now the load is a few dozen kilometers from the fighting, and a new question appears.
Who decides what goes to which unit?
There are two ways to run it.
In a push system, planners guess what the units will need, and send it forward regardless.
In a pull system, the units ask for what they want, and wait for it to arrive.
Both fail in a recognizable way.
Push delivers, with great efficiency, a palette of exactly the wrong thing.
Pull delivers the right thing, but late, because every request has to climb the chain, and every
answer has to come back down.
Modern armies mix the two, and most of the skill lies in deciding which items belong on
which side.
Fuel, ammunition, and water are pushed at a steady planned rate, because every unit uses
them.
Everything unusual is pulled.
The last stretch is the part nobody photographs.
A battalion in contact carries a basic load of ammunition on its own vehicles and cannot carry
much more.
So something has to refill it, usually at night, usually by a small group of trucks that
finds the unit, drops pallets, takes away empty containers and the wounded, and leaves
before dawn.
Every delivery is a small operation of its own, with a route to pick, a time to meet, and a
unit that may have moved since the order was written.
The truck that arrives is the end of a chain several thousand kumaners long, and if it does
not arrive, nothing that came before it matters.
Count what the people alone need, a soldier drinks several liters of water a day in a
hot climate and needs more again to wash and to cook, and a few thousand soldiers need
a tanker convoy for that and nothing else.
Fuel is the other giant.
In recent American operations, by some accounts fuel and water together made up the largest
share of everything shipped by weight, well ahead of ammunition, which is the cargo people
tend to picture.
Supply is only half of staying in the fight, because machines also break, and they break
far more often than the enemy destroys them.
A track snaps, an engine overheats, a gearbox gives up after a week of hard use on bad ground.
Armies handle that with tiers of repair.
The crew fixes what it can with tools on its own vehicle, such as a wheel or a track link.
The battalion workshop handles bigger faults, and increasingly it does not repair a part at
all.
It swaps the whole assembly, so a tank's engine and transmission, the power pack, can be lifted
out and replaced in a matter of hours.
The faulty one goes back to a depot far from the fighting, where it can be rebuilt with proper
tools and without anyone shooting at the mechanics.
Spare parts are a supply problem too, and a quietly cruel one.
A vehicle worth millions can sit in a field for weeks because of a part that costs a few hundred.
Wartime armies learn to cannibalize, taking one broken vehicle apart to keep two others
running, which is efficient and also a little like eating your own furniture.
Whether that is a sensible choice depends on how many days the army expects to keep fighting
without the factory.
There is a common mistake in how people picture all this.
Logistics sounds like support, the dull tail behind the teeth that actually do the fighting.
It is closer to the reverse.
The tail decides where the teeth can go, how fast, and for how long.
A commander with a brilliant plan and no fuel has a plan for a place the army cannot reach.
Speed is not a quality of the tanks alone.
It is how fast the fuel can follow them.
There is a second mistake, which is believing that more stock is always safer.
A large depot is a large target.
Western and Ukrainian sources reported that in mid-2022, long-range strikes on Russian ammunition
stores near the front forced Russia to move them farther back, and Russian officials did
not confirm the detail.
If that is right, and this is an inference rather than a confirmed fact, then the strikes did
more than destroy ammunition.
They lengthened the road between the depot and the guns, which is exactly the trap of the
opening, applied by the enemy rather than by geography.
So come back to the truck that burns the fuel it carries.
Nobody ever solves that problem.
They move the depot, shorten the road, lay the pipe, swap the engine, and protect the one
thing that cannot be replaced fast, which is the chain itself.
An army is not the tanks it parades.
It is whatever is still arriving on the 10th day.
The end of the day is the engine that has got the vast damage that it weighs in on the 10th day.
